title.en: Kubiya, the Leper King in His Farm Hut
title.zh: 庫比亞——蟄居田舍的麻瘋王

region.en: Abeokuta district, Nigeria (the farm hut of the deposed king)
region.zh: 奈及利亞阿貝奧庫塔近郊（廢王蟄居的田舍）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: Two rival traditions explain Orisha Oko, the harvest god. In Keribo's account his name was Kubiya: he was a king and a tyrant, poisoned by one of his subjects and stricken with leprosy. His people built him a hut in the farm (oko), and as he was reluctant to leave home, kingly reverence was promised him in this retreat — a promise fulfilled, so that after his death men repair thither to worship him; the white and red marks used by his devotees indicate the chalk and camwood he is in the habit of using to conceal the leprous spots in their initial stage. In another account his name was again Kubiya, but he was a trapper of guinea fowls who became an extraordinary physician and diviner, called Orisa-Oko, the village god, because he lived in a village.
summary.zh: 關於農耕神奧里莎奧科有兩種說法。柯里博記載：他本名庫比亞，是位暴君，被臣下毒害而染麻瘋。族人為他在田中（奧科）搭起茅舍；他不願遠離家園，人們便許諾在此奉他為王——諾言果然兌現，他死後世人至今前往其舍祭拜。信眾額上、身上的白紅斑記，正是他用白堊與紅木粉遮掩初期麻瘋斑點的遺痕。另一說他名叫庫比亞，原是捕珠雞的獵手，後成醫術通神的名醫與占者；因住在村中而被稱為「奧里莎奧科」——村落之神。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; rival euhemeristic traditions for the harvest god collected by Dennett. Leprosy described as the recorded tradition states it, respectfully. Cross-ref: yoruba-orisa-oko-demon-polo, yoruba-orisa-oko-witch-cave.

passages.text: His name was Kubiya. He was a king and a tyrant. He was poisoned by one of his subjects and was leprous. His people thereafter built him a hut in the farm (oko), and as he was reluctant to leave home, kingly reverence was promised him in this retreat. This promise was fulfilled, so that after his death men repair thither to worship him. The white and red marks used by its devotees indicate the chalk and camwood he is in the habit of using to conceal the leprous spots in their initial stage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Orisha Oko's name was Kubiya. His first occupation was to catch wild guinea fowls and sell them. He afterwards became a physician, and was such an extraordinary man that his powers were considered supernatural. He resided in a village where all men came to him, for he was a very skilful medical man and diviner. He was called Orisa-Oko (village god) because he lived in a village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Oke Visits Men in Dreams to Fix the Rain-Feast

region.en: Ibadan, Nigeria (the hill-goddess who commands the drought festival)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊巴丹（吩咐旱祭日期的山神）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: The Orisha Oke may well be called the titular goddess of Ibadan: when the chiefs were asked what emblem should figure on the medals of their agricultural show, they unanimously selected Oke, photographed as a fine-looking woman, her breasts exposed and her arms raised towards heaven as if to welcome her children — a picture of fruitfulness. She is the hill Orisha connected with fire; her festival used to be held when the land was at its driest and rain was most required to quench its thirst. She would appear to a man in a dream and tell him to go to the Bale and ask him to fix a day for the feast; if the Bale took no notice, she would visit another man in a dream; if the Bale hesitated she threatened to send fire down from heaven to burn his house. Her demands varied — sometimes a man as a sacrifice, sometimes 200 pigeons, sometimes a bullock or a sheep — and on the festival day no trade was done, and anyone coming into the town was robbed of all he brought.
summary.zh: 山神奧凱堪稱伊巴丹的守護女神：酋長們為農業賽會的獎章選徽記時，不約而同選中奧凱——一位豐滿美婦的形象，袒露雙乳、雙臂高舉向天，如迎自己的兒女——一幅豐饒之圖。她是與火相連的山嶽之神；她的祭典總在大地最乾渴、最盼雨時舉行。她會在夢中向某人顯現，命他去請巴萊（村長）定下祭日；巴萊若置之不理，她便託夢另一人再去催請；巴萊若仍遲疑，她便威脅降天火焚其宅。她的索求時而是一名活人為祭，時而是二百隻鴿子，時而是一頭牛或一隻羊。祭日當天全城罷市，誤入城中者財物盡失。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910. Dennett also describes a licensed festival attached to this rite; that material is summarized in the corpus only in its ritual-and-rain aspects, without explicit description. Human sacrifice demands reported as the recorded tradition states it.

passages.text: The Orisha Oke may well be called the titular goddess of Ibadan. When the chiefs of that place were asked what animal or sign they would like as an emblem to figure on the medals to be given away at their agricultural show, they unanimously selected Oke. They had the photograph of a fine looking woman taken, her breasts exposed, and her arms raised towards heaven, as if to welcome her children — a picture of fruitfulness. She is the hill Orisha, connected with fire. Her festival used to be held when the land was at its driest and rain was most required to quench its thirst.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: She would appear to a man in a dream and tell him to go to the Bale and ask him to fix a day for the feast. Perhaps the Bale would take no notice, and then she would visit another man in a dream and ask him to go. If the Bale hesitated, she threatened to send fire down from heaven to burn his house and cause him a great loss. She sometimes demanded a man as a sacrifice, sometimes 200 pigeons, sometimes a bullock or a sheep. Notice would be sent round to all the villages and the day stated; everyone had to be in the town the day before the date fixed, and anyone coming into the town on the day of the festival would be robbed of all he might be bringing with him. No trade was done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sixteen Odus as the Order of Propagation

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the diviner's tray at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費的占卜托板）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XV

summary.en: Dennett took the order of the Ifa odus from an Ifa priest, Oliyitan, verified three months later, and read them as the order of propagation: Iroshun and Owourin, filtration and drizzle — water; Obara, that which bears the oil seed — earth; Okoron, the dry bed of a river, and Oguda, that which pounds and creates marriage; Osa, that which dries and evaporates — loss; Ika, he who reaps, and Oturupon, he who gathers — first harvest, the conception of man; Otura and Irete, ease, happiness and hope, when there is no anxiety about food — pregnancy; Oshe, that which shall be — emission; Ofu, to appear in the wrong month without being expected — pain, suffering, travail. The categories of creation, reproduction, death and salvation he found at the back of the Yoruba babalawo's mind as well as the Congolese.
summary.zh: 德內特向伊法祭司奧利伊坦請得十六奧杜之序，三月後再問，次序絲毫不差。他將其讀作孕育之序：伊羅舜與奧烏林——滲濾與細雨，屬水；奧巴拉——負油之種，屬土；奧科隆（乾涸河床）與奧古達（舂捣而造）——論婚嫁；奧薩——曬乾蒸發，屬損耗；伊卡（收割者）與奧圖魯彭（聚合者）——初獲，即人的受孕；奧圖拉與伊雷特——安然、喜樂與盼望，無糧食之憂，即懷孕之期；奧謝——將至之事，即臨盆；奧富——不期而至於不當之月，即陣痛與分娩之苦。他認為創造、孕育、死亡與救贖的次序，同樣潛藏於約魯巴巴巴拉奧與剛果巫祝的心底。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; Dennett's structural reading of the Ifa odu sequence (his interpretation, reported as such). Complements the Johnson and Frobenius accounts of Ifa's corpus. Cross-ref: yoruba-opele-servant-oracle.

passages.text: I obtained the order of the Odus from Oliyitan, an Ifa priest, and to make sure that the order was correct so far as he was concerned, I asked him to give me the order again about three months afterwards. As it was exactly the same I have adopted this as correct.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Taking the order as given to me by the babalawo, and remembering the order of the seasons, there can be no doubt that they tell us of the order of propagation: Iroshun, filtration, and Owourin, that which drizzles — water; Obara, that which bears the oil seed — earth; Okoron, the dry bed of a river, and Oguda, that which pounds and creates — marriage; Osa, that which dries and evaporates — loss; Ika, he who reaps, harvest, and Oturupon, he who gathers — the first harvest, man's conception; Otura and Irete, translated to me as ease, happiness, hope, when there is no anxiety about food, a time of fruitfulness — the time when the woman shows signs of pregnancy and she is happy and hopeful; Oshe, that which shall be — emission; Ofu, to appear in the wrong month without being expected — pain, suffering, travail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the King's courtyard where the broken world-calabash was mended)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（修補破碎天地葫蘆的王宮前庭）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett, from Mr. George)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XV, quoting the story of the breaking of Igba at Ife

summary.en: All the world met in the King's courtyard to discuss the breaking of the world-renowned Igba, the calabash of Ife — Heaven and Earth in one shell. They called Awlawta to put it together again, but he could not; Beni-ado of Ife and Owo of Otu; Ogun also was sent for, which means war was declared over the breakage — but none of them could put the calabash together again. People farmed and waited for the rain, but none came; then hunger came, and man and beast mourned for their dead. Obalufon from Iyinde, Laberinjo from Ido, Jigure from Otun Moba, Esegba an Egba, Asadu from Ijesa, Akoda from Ife, Aseda Araba the law-giving cotton tree their father, Olumo from Imori, Ogun of Alara, Ogbon of Ijero, and Odudugbundu of Eshemaiva, the father devil who lived in Ketu — all these could do nothing. Then Ototo Enia, the truthful one, blew his trumpet — the elephant ran to the bush, the wild ox to its field, the rat to its hole, beans to the brook, the dog to the land of meditation, the sheep to the country of stupidity, all beasts to beastland — and Ajalaiye, Ajalorun, and Ajirilogbon were called. The people confessed their filth and prayed that the broken calabash might be patched; Ajirilogbon told them to find the leaf of a tree called Ewe-Alashuwalu, capable of remodelling a man's evil character; they could not find it, so he took it out of the bag of Egede, the bag of deep mystery, and mended the broken Igba of Ife — and rain fell, and healed all the people, and stopped the calamity from causing further harm.
summary.zh: 聞名天下的伊費葫蘆「伊格巴」——合天地於一殼——忽然破碎，萬民齊聚王宮前庭商議。請阿烏拉塔來修，修不好；伊費的貝尼-阿多、奧圖的奧沃也請來了；連奧貢都請動了——意味著為此碎裂而宣戰——依然無人能將葫蘆復原。人們照常耕作、盼雨，雨卻不來；接著饑荒降臨，人獸同哀亡者。伊延德的奧巴魯豐、伊多的拉貝林喬、奧圖莫巴的吉古雷、埃格巴人埃塞格巴、伊傑薩的阿薩杜、伊費的阿科達、「賜法木棉」阿塞達-阿拉巴（眾人之父）、伊莫里的奧盧莫、阿拉拉的奧貢、伊傑羅的奧貢、以及居於凱圖的眾魔之父奧杜格本杜——全都無能為力。此時「誠實者」奧托托-埃尼亞吹響號角：大象奔入林、野牛歸田、老鼠入洞、豆落溪、犬往冥想之鄉、羊往愚魯之國，眾獸各歸獸國——接著「與地上事務角力者」阿賈拉伊耶、「與天界事務角力者」阿賈洛倫、「司視與智慧者」阿吉里洛貢被一一請到。民眾懺悔罪污，求補破葫蘆；阿吉里洛貢命他們尋一種能重塑人的惡習的樹葉「埃韋-阿拉舒瓦盧」；眾人尋不得，他便從「埃格德」——深奧之秘的袋子——中取出此葉，補好了伊費的碎葫蘆。雨隨即落下，醫愈萬民，災殃自此不再蔓延。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910 by Dennett from Mr. George's account; the fall-and-restoration of the Ife calabash (Heaven-and-Earth shell), with the famine that follows its breaking. Dennett notes the Humpty Dumpty parallel. Cross-refs: yoruba-odudua-blind-calabash, yoruba-olokun-flood-chained.

passages.text: They called Awlawta to come and put it together again, but he could not. Beni ado from Ife, and Owo from Otu were called. Ogun also is sent for; which means that war was declared over this breakage. But none of them could put the calabash together again. People farmed and waited for the rain, but none came. Then hunger came, and man and beast mourned for their dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Obalufon from Iyinde, Laberinjo from Ido, Jigure from Otun Moba, Esegba an Egba, Asadu from Ijesa, Akoda from Ife, Aseda Araba (the law-giving cotton tree), their father, Olumo from Imori, Ogun of Alara, Ogbon of Ijero, Odudugbundu of Eshemaiva, the father devil who lived in Ketu — but all these could do nothing. They call Akonilogbon and Afonahanni and ask their assistance; they advised them to call in Ototo Enia, the truthful one. From the beginning at the creation of the world this duty of trumpeter to the man from heaven was specially laid on him. Then he blew his trumpet, and the elephant went quickly to the Eselu bush, the wild ox to Elugu apako, the bird Kekeke flies to the ale plant, the rat runs to its hole, the beans to the brook, the dog to the land of meditation, the sheep to the country of stupidity — all beasts go to beastland, beings go to the land of beings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ajalaiye, he who strives with earthly affairs; Ajalorun, he who strives with heavenly affairs; Ajirilogbon, he who strives with matters concerning sight and wisdom, were called. The people confess their filth and pray that he should patch the broken calabash, and Ajirilogbon tells them to go and find the leaf of a tree called Ewe-Alashuwalu (which is said to be capable of remodelling a man's evil character). They cannot find it. He then takes it out of the bag of Egede (the bag of deep mystery), and mends the broken Igba of Ife, and rain falls, and so heals all the people, and stops the calamity from causing further harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XV (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Idowu Recites the Names of Shango

region.en: Oyo and Akure, Nigeria (the festival procession of the Odushushango)
region.zh: 奧約與阿庫雷（尚戈男信眾的祭典行列）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: Jakuta is the name of Shango's day: Shango is the Alafin of Oyo's great Orisha and is sometimes called Oba Kuso, the king of Kuso, a hill near Oyo sacred to him. An Odushushango named Idowu recited his names: Alada Ogun, the one who splits the mortar that Ogun is said to wear on his head; Ako aja abinrinja lese, the he-dog that walks as one about to fight; Aja jumoni koto kpanije, the one who frightens one before he kills and eats him; Olilu tun ilu re she, one who puts his town in order; Ebi ti ka waw ponyin shoro, the one who with his hands behind his back does him an injury; Akuwarapa abija kaka, the one who has fits and is extraordinarily strong. His wife Oya runs on ahead when Shango goes out to fight, the strong tornado wind; Oshun is the gathering darkness and Oba the wild clouds that meet — these two stay at home to keep house. His sacred tree is the Ayan, from which his staff is made; his food taboos (ewaws) are the Sese beans, the Eligidi pumpkin, the Esuro antelope, the Ekun rabbit, and the Eku-ago, the white-bellied rat which the Alafin of Oyo is seen at times to raise to his lips as if to kiss.
summary.zh: 「賈庫塔」是尚戈的聖日之名；尚戈是奧約阿勞芬的大神，又稱「奧巴庫索」——庫索王，即奧約附近獻給他的聖山。尚戈男信眾（奧杜舒尚戈）伊多沃誦其諸名：奧拉達奧貢（劈開奧貢頭上木杵者）；如欲鬥之犬而行的公犬；先嚇後殺的噬人者；整飭其城者；反手傷人者；癲狂而神力無匹者。其妻奧雅是尚戈出征時一馬當先的龍捲狂風；奧舜是聚攏的黑暗，奧巴是相撞的烏雲——此二人留守家中。其聖樹為阿揚木（神杖即取材於此）；其食忌為塞塞豆、南瓜、羚羊、野兔，以及白腹鼠——奧約阿勞芬時而把它舉到唇邊，彷彿親吻。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the praise-name roll and food taboos of Shango's cult, complementing Ellis's chant (yoruba-shango-fiery-stones) and Frobenius's ram cycle (yoruba-shango-ram-thunderbolt).

passages.text: Jakuta is the name of Shango's day. Shango is the Alafin of Oyo's great Orisha and is sometimes called Oba Kuso, the king of Kuso, a hill near Oyo which is sacred to him. His male followers are called Odushushango and the female Esin nla (the great horse). An Odushushango named Idowu gave the following information: another name is Alada Ogun, the one who splits the mortar that Ogun is said to wear on his head; Ako aja abinrinja lese, the he-dog that walks as one about to fight; Aja jumoni koto kpanije, the one who frightens one before he kills and eats him; Olilu tun ilu re she, one who puts his town in order; Ebi ti ka waw ponyin shoro, the one who with his hands behind his back does him an injury; Akuwarapa abija kaka, the one who has fits and is extraordinarily strong.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife Oya is she who runs on ahead when Shango goes out to fight, the strong tornado wind. Oshun is the gathering darkness and Oba the wild clouds that meet. These two stay at home to keep house. They sacrifice the cow, the sheep and the cock to Shango. His sacred tree is the Ayan from which his staff is made. His ewaws (food taboos) are the Sese (beans), the Eligidi (pumpkin), the Esuro (antelope), the Ekun (rabbit), and the Eku ago or white-bellied rat which the Alafin of Oyo is seen at times to raise to his lips as if to kiss.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Naming the Child's Guardian Orisha: Footprints of Fate
title.zh: 為嬰孩問出守護神——命運的足印

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the naming-day threshold near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊命名日的門前）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. XVI

summary.en: From marriage to birth there are no Orisha ceremonies; but when the child is born the parents ask the priest to what Orisha they owe this good fortune, and when he tells them they sacrifice to it. Three days after the birth they call in the priest and ask him to name the child's Ese entele — its footprints: the babalawo consults Ifa, and as the priest mentions an Orisha, shakes his head until that which is to become the guardian spirit of the child is mentioned. The child, as soon as it is able, fetches water for this Orisha and sacrifices to it on all great occasions during its life; if Obatala is the Orisha, the child must wear white and must not drink palm wine nor eat dog. The grandparents as well as the parents each thank their separate Orishas on the safe delivery; if a girl, a name is given on the seventh day, if a boy, on the ninth.
summary.zh: 自婚至產並無奧里莎之儀；孩子降生後，父母便請祭司指點：此番好運該歸功於哪位神？指明之後便向祂獻祭。產後三日請祭司為孩子問出「埃塞恩特勒」——命運的足印：巴巴拉奧求問伊法，祭司逐一念神名，直到搖出將成為孩子守護神的那一位為止。孩子稍長，便為這位奧里莎取水、逢大典獻祭；若守護神是奧巴塔拉，孩子終身必穿白衣、不得飲棕櫚酒、不得食犬。平安產後，祖輩與父母各自感謝自己的守護神；女嬰第七日命名，男嬰第九日。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the life-cycle rite of guardian-orisha attribution, reported from the marriage-birth chapter of Dennett's informants (Odedaino).

passages.text: From the time of marriage to the time of birth there are no Orisha ceremonies, but when the child is born they ask the priest to what Orisha they owe this good fortune, and when he tells them they sacrifice to it. Three days after the birth they call in the priest and ask him to name the child's Ese entele, or footprints. The babalawo consults Ifa, who, as the priest mentions an Orisha, shakes his head until that which is to become the guardian spirit of the child is mentioned. The child, as soon as it is able, fetches water for this Orisha and sacrifices to it on all great occasions during its life. If Obatala is the Orisha then the child must wear white and must not drink palm wine nor eat dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: The grandparents as well as the parents on the safe delivery of their child each thank their separate Orishas. The priest gives the mother medicine for the preservation of the child. If it be a girl, a name is given to it on the seventh day; if a boy, on the ninth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. XVI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: The Koran on the Peg: How the Worship of Odudua Began
title.zh: 釘上的《可蘭經》——奧杜杜瓦崇拜之源

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the wall where the bag hung)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（掛袋的牆壁）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1910 (Dennett, from F. S.)

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VI

summary.en: Many years after the death of Odudua, a Hausa Mussulman came to Ife. He used to call the inhabitants together and read to them passages from the copy of the Koran which he brought with him, saying in imperfect Yoruba: "Let us worship Allah; He created the Mountain, He created the lowland, He created everything, He created us." He did this from time to time without gaining a single proselyte, and died a few months after his arrival. After his death his Koran was found hanging on a peg on the wall in a bag; some of the men who saw it said: "The late Hausaman told us this was the personage who created existence — this is Odudua; let us therefore worship him" — misunderstanding the Mussulman. So they removed the bag containing the Koran from the peg, put it on the ground, covered it with a pot and began to worship it: so commenced the worship of Odudua.
summary.zh: 奧杜杜瓦逝世多年之後，一位豪薩回教徒來到伊費。他召集居民，向他們誦讀隨身攜帶的《可蘭經》，並用生硬的約魯巴語說：「讓我們拜安拉吧——祂造了高山，祂造了窪地，祂造了萬物，祂造了我們。」他屢屢宣講，卻未得一個皈依者，來後數月便去世了。他死後，人們發現他的《可蘭經》用布袋裝著，掛在牆上的木釘上。有人便說：「那亡故的豪薩人告訴我們，此物就是那創造萬有的存在——這就是奧杜杜瓦，我們拜祂吧！」——他們誤解了那位回教徒。於是眾人取下牆釘上的經袋，放在地上，用一口罐子罩住，開始崇拜——奧杜杜瓦的崇拜便由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910 from F. S.'s Nigerian Chronicle history; a Muslim-Yoruba contact legend explaining the origin of Odudua worship as a misunderstood Koran. Odudua's name glossed as Odu ti o da iwa, the personage who created existence; his wife Omonide means a child is brass.

passages.text: Many years after the death of Odudua a Hausa Mussulman came to Ife. He used to call the inhabitants together and read to them passages from the copy of the Koran which he brought with him from his country. He was wont to say to the people in Yoruba imperfectly as he could speak it with accents foreign to the language: "Let us worship Allah; He created the Mountain, He created the lowland, He created everything, He created us." He did this from time to time without being able to gain a single proselyte, and died a few months after his arrival in Ife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: After his death his Koran was found hanging on a peg on the wall where he had left it in a bag. Some of the men who saw it said: "The late Hausaman told us this was the personage who created existence; this is Odudua, let us therefore worship him" — misunderstanding the Mussulman. So they removed the bag containing the Koran from the peg on the wall, put it on the ground, covered it with a pot and began to worship it. So commenced the worship of Odudua.

title.en: Odudua Makes the Body; Obatala the Fingers, Eyes and Ears
title.zh: 奧杜杜瓦塑身，奧巴塔拉造目造指

region.en: Egba country, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the sculptor's shrine near Abeokuta)
region.zh: 奈及利亞埃格巴之地（象徵定位：阿貝奧庫塔附近的雕塑者聖所）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VII

summary.en: A story told by an Egba called Salako shows Obatala as the person who sensitises matter: he is the son of Odudua and was sent to do good on earth. When anyone is sick he tells them what leaf to get and they get well; if any woman wants a child, any leaf he cuts and gives to her has the desired effect. The people thanked Odudua for sending him, and said he was a good man. Then Odudua made the body of man and called Obatala to do the rest: Obatala made the fingers, the eyes, the mouth, the ears. Those who worship him call him Obatala to da oju, imu, eti, emi, ati apari shikokanlelogun — the Oba who makes the eyes, the mouth, the ears, the nose, and the skull to be, twenty-one. When he finished the work, Olodumare breathed into the body and it became a living being; Odudua gave orders to all the world to worship Obatala, and he is now Odudua's mason and sculptor. All things that Obatala and his followers wear are white — white chalk, beads, cap and cloth.
summary.zh: 埃格巴人薩拉科講的故事，把奧巴塔拉說成「賦物以靈」之人：他是奧杜杜瓦之子，奉命降世行善。人有病，他指點該採何種草藥，服之即癒；婦人求子，他剪贈一葉，便能如願。眾人感謝奧杜杜瓦遣他下凡，讚他是好人。其後奧杜杜瓦造出人的身體，喚奧巴塔拉續成其餘：手指、眼睛、口、耳皆他所造。信眾稱他「造眼、口、耳、鼻與頭骨者，二十一」。工程既畢，奧洛杜馬雷向身體吹入氣息，它便成了活人。奧杜杜瓦遂曉諭天下敬拜奧巴塔拉——他如今是奧杜杜瓦的石匠與雕塑師。凡奧巴塔拉及其信眾所用皆白：白堊、白珠、白帽、白衣。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the body-making myth in Dennett's version (Odudua fashions, Obatala finishes, Olodumare quickens) — complementary to the clay-molding traditions. Cross-refs: obatala-creation, obatala-alamorere, yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen.

passages.text: He is the son of Odudua, and was sent to do good on earth. When anyone is sick he will tell them what leaf to get and they will get well. If any woman wanted a child, any leaf he cut and gave to her would have the desired effect. Then the people thanked Odudua for sending him, and said he was a good man. Then Odudua made the body of man and called Obatala to do the rest, and so Obatala made the fingers, the eyes, the mouth, the ears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VII (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: They who worship him used to call him Obatala to da oju, imu, eti, emi, ati apari shikokanlelogun — Oba who makes the eyes, the mouth, the ears, the nose, and the skull to be, twenty-one. When he finished the work, Olodumare breathed into the body and it became a living being. And so Odudua gave orders to all the world to worship Obatala, and those who now worship him are the descendants of those who benefited by his goodness when he came on earth. And now he is Odudua's mason and sculptor. All things that Obatala and his followers wear are white — white chalk, beads, cap and cloth.

title.en: The Money Too White to Touch: Why Silver Is Called Fadaka
title.zh: 不敢觸碰的白錢——白銀何以名「法達卡」

region.en: Egba country, Nigeria (the town gate where the albino waited)
region.zh: 奈及利亞埃格巴之地（白化者守望的城門）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VII

summary.en: Mr. Pellegrin gave Dennett a story of Obatala as a king: he was the poorest of the four kings, and had bought an albino as a slave. When famine was raging he had nothing to eat, and he had a wife and child; so when they were starving he told the albino to go and find his own chop (food). The albino went crying about the streets and stood at the gate of the town, as some people with food might be coming. That day a European with his retinue came, accompanied by a dog; the dog, who came first and met the albino, was frightened and ran back to his master. The master came to find out what had frightened the dog, found the albino at the gate, heard his story, and asked Obatala why, if he had food for his wife and child, he had none for his slave. Told of the famine, the white man, seeing their condition, mixed some milk for them and stayed that night; next morning, going, he gave them food and money. Obatala called the slave to come and count it, but they did not dare to touch it, as it was too white — so they took a matchet to divide it: hence silver is called Fadaka.
summary.zh: 佩勒格林講述的奧巴塔拉為王的故事：他是四王之中最窮的一個，買了一名白化者為奴。饑荒之年，家有妻兒卻斷糧，他只得讓白化奴僕自尋吃食。奴僕沿街哭討，立於城門口，盼著有人攜食而來。那日恰有一位歐洲人攜僕從、帶著一隻狗到來；狗先到，見了白化人嚇得回奔主人。主人前來查看，聽完原委，便問奧巴塔拉：既有飯食與妻兒，何以無食與奴？得知饑荒實情，這位白人見其窘狀，為他們調了牛奶，留宿一夜；次日臨行，又留下食物與金錢。奧巴塔拉喚奴僕來清點——那錢太白了，他們竟不敢用手碰，只得取彎刀來分——白銀「法達卡」之名由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; hospitality-to-stranger tale with a money etiology, told of Obatala as one of four kings. Colonial-era European figure reported as the recorded story states it.

passages.text: Obatala was the poorest of the four Kings; he bought an Albino as a slave. And when famine was raging he had nothing to eat, and he had a wife and child; so when they were starving he told the Albino to go and find his own chop (food). He went crying about the streets. He stood at the gate of the town, as some people with food might be coming. That day a European with his retinue came accompanied by a dog. The dog, who came first and met the Albino, was frightened and ran back to his master. The master came to find out what had frightened the dog, and found the Albino at the gate. He asked him what was the matter, and he told him his story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VII (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the European asked him to take him to his master. And he asked Obatala why, if he had food for his wife and child, he had none for his slave? The master told him of the famine, and said he had sent the Albino to find his own chop. Then the white man, seeing their condition, mixed some milk for them and stayed that night. Next morning when going he gave them food and money, and left. Obatala called the slave to come and count it. But they did not dare to touch it, as it was too white, so they took a matchet to divide it, hence silver is called Fadaka.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VII (1910); not verbatim.
